newsitem.title: CANADA: Highlights of British Columbia forest jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of British Columbia forest jobs plan.

text.p: Following are highlights of a plan announced by British Columbia Premier Glen Clark to increase employment in the forestry industry.
-- The plan calls for the creation of 22,400 direct and 17,400 indirect new jobs in the sector by 2001.
-- The government will spend C$370 million a year on the initiatives. Of that, C$300 million would come from the Forest Renewal agency, which funds silviculture and other projects.
-- The government is spurring forestry companies to participate through a combination of incentives and penalties.

-- The plan calls for forestry companies to add 8,900 jobs directly. Of that amount, 3,900 would come from increased harvesting facilitated by a streamlining of government bureaucracy. Red tape has prevented companies from cutting their full allocations of wood and they face a backlog.

Another 3,000 jobs would be created after negotiations with the unions on reducing overtime and hours of work for existing employees. The government will spend C$20 million a year to offset additional payroll costs.
A further 2,000 jobs would come from capital investment to improve technological efficiency and developing higher value products and markets.
-- Forest Renewal programs will add 5,000 direct jobs in areas such as forest enhancement, resource inventories and watershed restoration.
-- Small forest enterprise and remanufacturing sectors would add 6,500 jobs.
-- Government programs to restore salmon streams in logging areas would create 2,000 jobs.
-- Breakdown of 17,400 spinoff jobs are 6,500 in small business and remanufacturing, 5,000 in forest renewal, 5,900 at forestry companies.

-- Small enterprise and remanufacturing plan requires major coastal lumber producers to offer 18 percent of sawn lumber to small secondary manufacturers at fair market prices. Interior lumber producers must offer 16 percent of sawn lumber to small businesses.

-- Of the total increase in direct jobs, 5,400 will stem from the streamlining of government bureacracy which has delayed logging. The steps seek to ensure industry has access to their full cut allocation. Government said over the past few years wood harvest has been three million cubic meters below the allowable cut.
Government also commits to review timber supply information and assess potential for increases.

-- The government through Forest Renewal will fund up to C$50 million a year for industry's incremental costs associated with Forest Practices Code logging rules on inventory, planning and road construction.
-- Companies that fail to deliver jobs "will be subject to sanctions that may include loss of access to innovative forest practices agreements and Forest Renewal funding."

-- Companies that create jobs will get priority access to Forest Renewal funding, eligibility for exemption from five percent "takeback" of annual cut when timber license is sold, priority for new forestry practices agreements and eligibility to carry forward undercut volumes where job creation can be demonstrated.

-- A jobs accord advocate will be named to monitor and report on progress. Companies will be required to report intentions of layoffs to advocate four months in advance and must show layoffs justified. New Forest Worker Agency will assist displaced workers. Details of agency to be negotiated by industry and unions on a regional basis.
